sections.title: Quick facts
sections.text: The ocellaris clownfish (Amphiprion ocellaris), or common clownfish, is a damselfish found on shallow Indo-West Pacific reefs. The November naturalist update reports a maximum length of about 4.3 inches and a depth range of roughly 3–60 feet. It feeds on small planktonic animals, including copepods, and algae.

sections.title: Life among stinging tentacles
sections.text: Watch a clownfish dart out and return to the anemone. The host’s stinging tentacles deter predators. The clownfish’s skin mucus helps it live among those tentacles, and the fish can defend its host by chasing away anemone-eating butterflyfishes. Dropped food and nutrients from fish waste can also benefit the host. Anemones have partnerships of their own. Algae living inside their tissues supply nutrients, and large anemones can shelter shrimp, crabs and several kinds of anemonefish. Research on clownfish mucus, including low levels of particular sialic acids, offers clues to how the fish may avoid triggering the anemone’s stinging cells. The roles of microbes and acclimation are still being investigated.

sections.title: Life cycle and sex change
sections.text: Clownfish are often described as all being born male. More precisely, they hatch sexually immature, and those that mature as breeders develop first as males. A typical group has one dominant breeding female, a smaller breeding male, and several smaller, immature fish. If the female dies or disappears, the breeding male can become the dominant female. The male tends the eggs near the host anemone, fanning them and removing compromised eggs. The November naturalist update reports about 100–1,000 eggs and hatching in roughly 6–8 days, depending on water temperature. After hatching, larvae drift before settling on a reef.

sections.title: Ocean in Motion · What to watch for
sections.text: Invite guests to watch for a fish peeking out between the tentacles. Ask where it goes when a larger fish swims past. For young visitors, try a game of peekaboo and then watch for the same movement in the exhibit.

sections.title: Conservation
sections.text: The Aquarium highlights the harm that chemical collection can cause to reef fishes and corals. For home aquariums, it recommends choosing captive-raised fish.
